\begin{chapteropening}

\section[-ai]{\mr{ै} — the ai vowel sign}

\label{lesson:MR-W59-ai-matra}



\begin{quote}
Three chapters ago you learned \textbf{\mr{ौ}} by adding a stroke to \textbf{\mr{ो}}. The same trick works one more time.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{ै}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{ै}} is \emph{ai}, and it is \textbf{\mr{े}} with a second stroke — the identical relationship \textbf{\mr{ौ}} has to \textbf{\mr{ो}}. Two marks, one rule, and with this one the four vowel signs of the \emph{e} and \emph{o} family are complete.

Hear them apart: \textbf{\mr{के}} is \emph{ke}; \textbf{\mr{कै}} is \emph{kai}, wider in the mouth. If you have met the pair \textbf{\mr{ो}} / \textbf{\mr{ौ}}, you already know what your voice has to do.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\mr{कै}} twice with the model visible. Then write \textbf{\mr{के}} beside it, and \textbf{\mr{को}} and \textbf{\mr{कौ}} underneath, and check that the second stroke falls in the same place in both pairs.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the difference between \textbf{\mr{े}} and \textbf{\mr{ै}}? (\textbf{One stroke}.) Which other pair works the same way? (\textbf{\mr{ो}} and \textbf{\mr{ौ}}.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A5\%88}{Devanagari ai vowel sign}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[paise]{\mr{पैसे} (paise) — money}

\label{lesson:MR-C59-paise}



\begin{quote}
You can count to twenty and you cannot name the one thing people count most often.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{पैसे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{पैसे}} — \emph{paise} — \textbf{money}
\end{quote}

The word the sign in the last lesson was for. \textbf{\mr{पैसे}} is Marathi's ordinary word for money, and it is \textbf{plural only} — there is no singular \emph{\mr{पैसा}} in this sense, the way English has no singular \emph{scissors}. You will always hear it and always say it in this shape.

Underneath it is the \textbf{paisa}, the coin that is a hundredth of a rupee, which is why the plural is the natural form: money is counted in many small pieces.

Now the numbers earn their keep. \textbf{\mr{किती} \mr{पैसे}?} — \emph{how much money?} — is the question the speaking paper's transactional part is built on, and you have owned \textbf{\mr{किती}} since chapter thirty-seven with nothing to ask it about.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{paise} — money
  \item \emph{kitī paise?} — how much money?
  \item \emph{mājhyākaḍe vīs paise āhet} — I have twenty
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What shape is \textbf{\mr{पैसे}} always in? (\textbf{Plural}.) Which sign did it need? (\textbf{\mr{ै}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AA\%E0\%A5\%88\%E0\%A4\%B8\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \mr{पैसे}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rupayā]{\mr{रुपया} (rupayā) — rupee}

\label{lesson:MR-C59-rupaya}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{पैसे}} is money in general. No price is ever quoted in it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{रुपया}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{रुपया}} — \emph{rupayā} — \textbf{rupee}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{वीस} \mr{रुपये}} — \emph{vīs rupaye} — \textbf{twenty rupees}
\end{quote}

This is the word a price is named in, and it is masculine, so it takes a plural ending after a number: one \textbf{\mr{रुपया}}, twenty \textbf{\mr{रुपये}}. Say the pair out loud until the change is automatic, because a number is almost never said without it.

The history is a good one. Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{रूप्य}} (\emph{rūpya}) meant \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{wrought silver}\textquotedblright{} — silver that had been given a SHAPE, from \textbf{\mr{रूप}} (\emph{rūpa}), \emph{form}. A rupee is, at root, shaped metal. The same coin name travelled out of India far enough that it is now the currency of half a dozen countries.

With a number in front of it you can finally answer the transactional part of the speaking paper: \textbf{\mr{किती}?} — \textbf{\mr{वीस} \mr{रुपये}}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{rupayā}, then \emph{vīs rupaye} — and hear the ending change
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kitī rupaye?} — how many rupees?
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{\mr{इ}} and name a word it opens
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \textbf{\mr{रूप्य}} mean in Sanskrit? (\textbf{Wrought silver} — shaped metal.) What happens to \textbf{\mr{रुपया}} after a number? (\textbf{It becomes \mr{रुपये}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B0\%E0\%A5\%81\%E0\%A4\%AA\%E0\%A4\%AF\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \mr{रुपया}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kitī rupaye?]{A price asked and answered}

\label{lesson:MR-R59-what-it-costs}



\begin{quote}
Twenty numbers, a word for money and a word for the currency. That is a whole exchange, and it is the first one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kitī rupaye?} — and answer with any number to twenty
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mājhyākaḍe paise āhet} — I have money
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ek} … \emph{vīs} once more, and stop where the book stops
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ithe} — here
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word names the currency and which names money in general? (\textbf{\mr{रुपया}}; \textbf{\mr{पैसे}}.) How far can you count? (\textbf{To twenty}.) Then stop.
\end{tcolorbox}
